m:baixa: Free to walk around. There's almost always a queue at the Elevador de Santa Justa: it's often better to look at it from outside.
m:chiado: The streets are steep and paved with smooth stone: wear shoes with good soles. The Bairro Alto is livelier in the evening; by day it's quiet.
m:alfama: The Sé is free, with hours that change with services. The Feira da Ladra flea market is on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Watch out for pickpockets on tram 28 and at crowded viewpoints.
m:castelo: Ticket €15. Until 31 October open 9am–9pm (last entry 8:30pm); from 1 November 9am–6pm (last entry 5:30pm). The walls and towers close earlier, about half an hour before the rest. The museum inside is closed for works.
m:belem: The monastery and the tower are closed on Mondays; the Belém Tower is being restored and may close at times. Entry to the tower costs €8, the Padrão about €6. From outside you can see everything for free.
m:jeronimosins: Ticket about €18 (guides give €18–21: check the website). Open Tuesday to Sunday; from October to April 10am–5:30pm, last entry 5pm; closed on Mondays. The church can be visited for free from the side entrance.
m:gulbenkian: Ticket €16 (includes the Founder's Collection and the modern collection, reopened in July 2026); closed on Tuesdays; open Wednesday–Monday 10am–6pm. On Sundays from 2pm entry is free. Hours are those stated by guides: check gulbenkian.pt.
m:cais: The Time Out Market is convenient but pricier than neighbourhood places: to eat cheaply, choose the nearby streets. The Ascensor da Bica is covered by the day ticket.
vd:confeitaria: A historic 1829 pâtisserie on the square, with glass-and-wood display cases: egg sweets, pastéis de nata and, in winter, the Christmas bolo-rei. The counter is handy for a coffee standing up.
vp:confeitaria: A pastry with coffee is under €6 (menu not seen).
vd:fabrica: An artisan coffee roaster a short walk from Rossio: specialty coffee, toast and baked goods, for a quiet breakfast away from the tourist spots.
vd:bifanas: A tiny Baixa shop that makes bifanas: hot rolls with a slice of marinated pork, Lisbon's fast food. Eaten standing at the counter.
vp:bifanas: A bifana usually costs €3–4 (menu not seen). Closed on Sundays, Saturday mornings only.
vd:alentejo: A Moorish-style palace with an azulejo courtyard, home of the Alentejo association, with a restaurant serving food from southern Portugal: generous portions and home-style prices.
vp:alentejo: A dish usually costs €10–15 (menu not seen).
vd:manteigaria: The pâtisserie for freshly baked pastéis de nata: the custard is made in view and you eat them warm, with a coffee at the counter. Open until midnight.
vp:manteigaria: A pastel de nata costs about €1.50 (menu not seen).
vd:trevo: A neighbourhood café-pâtisserie on Largo Camões: breakfasts, toast, bifana or prego (beef steak roll) sandwiches and Portuguese pastries.
vp:trevo: A sandwich or a full breakfast is under €9 (menu not seen).
vd:kristof: Specialty coffee and a small kitchen in Príncipe Real, with a simple brunch menu: filter coffee, toast and cakes. Open on weekdays only.
vd:flores: A small tasca in the Chiado: sharing plates (petiscos) on a menu that changes daily, in a room with a few tables. No bookings and cash only, so you often wait outside.
vp:flores: Three or four petiscos to share are around €12–15 per person (menu not seen). Hours shown are Monday's.
vd:ze: A Mouraria tasca with a long shared table and grilled pork ribs. No bookings and cash only: arrive early or queue.
vp:ze: The grilled ribs cost about €12; dinner is only Thursday to Saturday.
vd:jaime: A neighbourhood tasca in Graça, with simple Portuguese dishes and a local crowd. Cash only, no bookings.
vp:jaime: A dish usually costs under €12 (menu not seen).
vd:pasteis: The 1837 pâtisserie where the pastel de nata was born, with a secret recipe: the queue at the entrance moves fast and there are many rooms of tables inside. Eat them with cinnamon and icing sugar.
vp:pasteis: A pastel costs about €1.50 (menu not seen). In summer it closes at 10pm.
vd:manteigariab: Manteigaria's Belém branch, a few steps from the monastery: freshly made pastéis de nata, with less of a queue than the historic shop.
vp:manteigariab: A pastel costs about €1.50 (menu not seen).
vd:comoba: Specialty coffee and a small bakery in Cais do Sodré, with outdoor tables: simple breakfasts and brunches to start the day.
vd:janis: A café open from breakfast to midnight, a short walk from the Time Out Market: sandwiches, toast and simple dishes at fair prices, handy at any hour.
vp:janis: A sandwich or a dish is usually under €12 (menu not seen).
vd:dear: A breakfast and brunch café in Bica, near the Ascensor: eggs, toast, cakes and hot drinks.
vd:solepesca: The tinned fish bar on Rua Nova do Carvalho (Pink Street): tins of tuna, sardines and mackerel served with bread and wine, in a reinvented fishermen's bar.
vp:solepesca: A tin with bread usually costs €6–10 (menu not seen). Hours Tuesday to Saturday: Sunday and Monday to be confirmed.
cd:oceanario: One of Europe's largest aquariums: a huge central tank with sharks, manta rays and sunfish.
cd:azulejo: Five centuries of painted tiles in a former convent, with a 23-metre panel of the city before the earthquake.
cd:panteao: The Baroque church with the white dome, where presidents and poets rest, with a terrace over the Alfama.
cd:mnaa: Portugal's most important art museum: Bosch, Dürer and the Japanese screens.
cd:santajusta: The 1902 iron lift linking the Baixa to the Chiado, with a viewpoint at the top.
cd:carmo: The ruins of a Gothic church left roofless since the 1755 earthquake.
cd:fado: The story of fado told through voices, guitars and old photos, in the heart of the Alfama.
cd:maat: The wave-shaped museum on the Tagus, with a roof you can walk on to see the river.
cd:zoolx: The zoo with a cable car and dolphin shows.
cd:se: The cathedral's Romanesque cloister with archaeological excavations.
